Threat.value: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room

vignette: Dr. Le had always been meticulous about her work as a dentist, known for her attention to detail and gentle touch with nervous patients. But it was outside of the office that her life began to unravel. Three years ago, she started noticing strange occurrences - a familiar face lurking in the parking lot, mysterious phone calls with no one on the other end, and an unsettling sense of being watched. It turned out that an ex-patient had become fixated on her, showing up at her home and office, leaving disturbing gifts and messages. As the stalking continued, Dr. Le found herself becoming increasingly vigilant. She would scan the waiting room before starting her day, searching for a familiar face or an unusual behavior. The sound of sirens outside her window made her jump, and she couldn't shake off the feeling that something was off. Certain songs that used to be her favorite now sent shivers down her spine - the same ones the stalker would play in his car when he followed her home. The police were involved, but Dr. Le found it difficult to trust their reassurances of safety. Even with a restraining order in place, she couldn't help but feel like she was constantly looking over her shoulder. She began to choose seats in restaurants and coffee shops based on how safe or protected she felt - always opting for the back corner where she could see everyone around her. Her friends and family thought she was being paranoid, but Dr. Le knew that this sense of hypervigilance was what kept her alive. At work, Dr. Le's usual composure started to slip. She would freeze during procedures if a patient mentioned something that triggered a memory of the stalker. The sound of a particular song on the radio or a news report about stalking cases would send her mind racing back to those terrifying months. Her patients began to notice the change in her demeanor, and some even commented on it. Despite her best efforts, Dr. Le couldn't shake off the feeling that she was in constant danger. She started to avoid certain routes home from work, opting for longer but safer paths. Her relationships with friends and family suffered as she became increasingly isolated. Even when her husband tried to reassure her that everything would be okay, Dr. Le just couldn't believe it. Now, three years after the stalking began, Dr. Le is at a breaking point. She can no longer keep up the facade of normalcy, and the constant fear has taken a toll on her mental health. She's started to see a therapist, hoping to learn how to manage these crippling symptoms and find some semblance of peace in her life again. As she sat in the waiting room for her first appointment, Dr. Le felt a familiar twinge of anxiety - would this be another place where she couldn't feel safe?
